explain: _sē_ points back to the subject of its own sentence: “himself, herself, itself, themselves”. It has no nominative.
distractors: _eī_ is “to him”. “Himself” as the thing loved is accusative _sē_.

explain: For I and you, the ordinary pronouns do the reflexive job: _mē_ (myself), _tē_ (yourself). Only the third person has _sē_.
distractors: _sē_ is for he, she, they. Here the subject is “I”: _mē_.
_sē_ is for he, she, they. Here the subject is “you”: _tē_.

explain: _sibi_ is the dative of _sē_: “to himself, for himself, to themselves”. The giver and the receiver are the same person.
distractors: _eī_ is “to him”, someone else. For the same person, _sibi_.
_sē_ is accusative. The one receiving is dative: _sibi_.

explain: _cum_ joins to the end of the pronouns: _sēcum_ (with himself), like _mēcum_ and _tēcum_.
distractors: _cum eō_ is “with him”, another person. “With himself” is the one word _sēcum_.

explain: _suus_ means “his own, her own, their own”: it belongs to the subject. It agrees with _fīlium_ (masculine accusative).
distractors: _eius_ means “his” as someone else’s son. For his own, use _suum_.
_suī_ is genitive or plural. _fīlium_ is accusative singular: _suum_.

en: He loves his son (a different man’s son).
explain: When “his” means another person’s, Latin uses _eius_, not _suus_. _suus_ would mean the subject’s own.
distractors: _suum_ would be his own son. This sentence means another man’s son: _eius_.
_suam_ is feminine accusative, and _suus_ means his own anyway: _eius_.
_eī_ is dative (“to him”). “His” is the genitive: _eius_.

explain: _suam_ agrees with _fīliam_ (feminine accusative). _suus_ takes its gender and case from the noun, not from the owner.
distractors: _suī_ is masculine genitive or plural. _fīliam_ is feminine singular: _suam_.

explain: _suōs_ agrees with _fīliōs_ (masculine accusative plural). The owners are “they”, so _suus_, not _eōrum_.
_sē_ is the same for singular and plural: himself or themselves. The soldiers defend the soldiers.
